label: Photograph
title: Photograph / 20:46
lines: The print shows your face beneath the station clock. Someone has written 20:46 on the back: four minutes after the death notice.
But the clock inside the photograph still reads 20:42. The negative envelope is dated tomorrow.
One image contradicts the registry, the clock, and its own date. Is that proof of you, or proof that this town edits its witnesses?
prompt: What will you let this photograph establish?
a: The registry erased me. The image is my witness.
b: Keep the contradiction. Neither source gets the last word.
resA: You accept the image as a witness, while keeping its impossible date attached. Trust is a decision, not a repair to the evidence.
resB: You preserve both incompatible times. You have found a reason to question the record, not a new authority to obey.

label: Radio
title: Radio / An unfinished warning
lines: A voice on the radio says: 'At 20:43 I saw you leave the square. I would know that coat anywhere.'
The sentence repeats. This time it ends: 'They gave me the coat before they gave me your name.'
Then a voice very like yours whispers: 'If you hear this, don't let a witness become another record you cannot question.'
a: A borrowed memory can still witness a living person.
b: A witness who learned my name may only remember a script.
resA: You keep the testimony without calling it certain. Someone else's memory can reach you even if you cannot verify its source.
resB: You record the voice and its rehearsed correction. Doubting a witness is different from deciding there was nobody to witness.

label: Stopped watch
title: Stopped watch / 20:42
lines: A watch is stopped at 20:42, the time printed on the death notice. The inside of its strap carries your initials.
It is warm. When you put it down, the second hand moves once, against the direction of the clock.
The watch agrees with the record. Your hand supplies the one thing the record cannot explain.
prompt: Which part of the watch belongs in your argument?
a: Agreement between two records deserves weight.
b: The warmth matters more than the matching time.
resA: You preserve the matching time, including the strange second that followed. Agreement is evidence; it is not immunity from doubt.
resB: You record what happened in your hand. The feeling could be false, but the record cannot replace the experience of having it.

label: Carbon copy
title: Registry / The copy underneath
lines: The upper page says: 'DECEASED. Entry finalized at 20:42.' The carbon copy beneath it says: 'ARRIVAL PENDING.'
Both pages carry the same stamp and signature. No one crossed out either version.
The office has not made one mistake. It has kept two official versions of you.
prompt: What does an institution's contradiction allow you to claim?
a: At least one official account must be wrong.
b: The accounts may describe different versions of me.
resA: You keep the duplicate stamp as evidence against certainty. Finding an error does not tell you which page deserves your trust.
resB: You leave room for incompatible versions. That possibility explains the paperwork, but it still cannot choose which life you will live.

label: Unsent letter
title: Unsent letter / In your handwriting
lines: 'I remember this street before the balconies were here. I remember writing the notice too.' The handwriting looks like yours.
The next sentence is unfinished: 'If I made the record, did I make the person it describes, or only the person who believed it?'
There is no signature. Someone has pressed the pen hard enough to mark the blank page underneath.
prompt: Is recognition enough to make this memory yours?
a: I recognize the hand. I will answer for what it wrote.
b: Recognition can be planted. I will keep the question open.
resA: You accept responsibility without claiming perfect memory. The unfinished question becomes something you can answer through what you do next.
resB: You keep the letter without turning familiarity into ownership. An uncertain memory can still be worth carrying.

label: Reserved seat
title: Reserved seat / Still waiting
lines: A reservation card says your seat will be held until 20:50. The station timetable says the last train left at 20:40.
Under the card, the wood has been worn smooth in the shape of a hand. Someone has waited here often.
A place can be kept for a person who will never come. Can it also keep a person from disappearing?
prompt: Does a place waiting for you count as a trace of you?
a: Being expected is a kind of belonging.
b: An empty place proves an expectation, not a person.
resA: You record the seat as a relation, not a certificate. It tells you that someone made room, even if you do not know for whom.
resB: You keep the reservation and its limit. The town can prepare a place without deciding who must occupy it.

label: Street plaque
title: Street plaque / A name underneath
lines: The sign reads 'RETURN STREET'. Under fresh paint, older letters spell 'DEPARTURE STREET'.
A small brass plate below it reads: 'Both routes are correct. Please use the current name.'
The road has not moved. Only its explanation has changed.
prompt: When the label changes, what are you willing to follow?
a: My remembered route, even if the town denies its name.
b: The road I can choose now, rather than either label.
resA: You record the earlier name. Your memory becomes one witness among others, with its own right to be questioned.
resB: You keep both names and refuse their instruction. The direction you take will be a fact of your action.

label: Departure ticket
title: Ticket / No destination
lines: The ticket is punched for tomorrow. Its destination field is blank. The passenger line contains your name.
Fine print: 'Passage does not certify the reality of the destination.' The return half has already been torn away.
A way out can be real without proving that what lies outside is more real.
prompt: Would you leave without a guarantee about the outside?
a: Yes. A choice can be mine without a promised answer.
b: No. Uncertainty does not make this place disposable.
resA: You keep the ticket as a permission, not a promise. Whatever waits outside will not retroactively make the choice for you.
resB: You record a reason to remain. Refusing the exit can be an act, rather than a failure to escape.

label: Fresh footprints
title: Footprints / A step not yet taken
lines: Two sets of footprints cross the dust. One matches your boots. The other stops exactly one step ahead of you.
A chalk note reads: 'The next step has already been filed.' There is room beside it for a different footprint.
If the town predicts the route, does walking it make you obedient? What would stepping aside actually prove?
prompt: Which action would you call your own?
a: Walk the predicted step because I choose it.
b: Step aside, even if the town records that too.
resA: You do not confuse agreement with an absence of choice. The question is who is deciding, not whether the result was expected.
resB: You keep the prediction as something you answered. A different footprint challenges the script without proving who wrote it.

label: Worn key
title: Worn key / A door remembered
lines: A worn key lies where an earlier marker promised 'proof'. It fits a small lock drawn on the wall, not an actual door.
Your fingers turn it before you remember why. The key's teeth have been filed down until almost any lock might accept it.
An object can feel personal because it belongs to you, or because somebody taught you how to hold it.
prompt: What do you keep from an object that cannot certify its owner?
a: The habit in my hand is a memory worth keeping.
b: The key is a possibility, not an identity document.
resA: You record the gesture as a memory, without asking the key to settle who you are.
resB: You keep what the key permits you to imagine. You need not prove ownership before deciding what to do with it.
